Risk analytics

How the numbers on the dashboard are calculated, and how well the model worked in the past.

Backtest: forecast VaR vs. realised {{H}}-day result

{{BT_CHART}}
{{BT_FULL}}

Method and comparison

Historical simulation: the last {{SCEN}} overlapping {{H}}-day changes of the ECB rate are applied to today's position. VaR is the loss exceeded in only 1% of these scenarios; Expected Shortfall is the average loss in the worst 2.5%.

{{TABLE}}
ApproachEUR% of position

Quote direction

The ECB quotes USD per 1 EUR. EUR value = USD {{USD}} / rate. A rising rate (stronger euro) lowers the EUR proceeds: loss = 1 − exp(−r), r = ln(St+5 / St).

Assumptions and limitations

  • The position is held for the full {{H}} trading days; conversion at the ECB reference rate, no bid/ask spread or fees.
  • History (3 years) is assumed to represent the next {{H}} days. Regime changes are not anticipated; the 1-year window is shown as a sensitivity.
  • Overlapping {{H}}-day windows share 4 of 5 days, so exceptions cluster and the Kupiec test is too optimistic. A non-overlapping check is shown under the backtest.
  • The Basel traffic light was designed for 1-day VaR; here it is a guide only.
  • Kupiec is two-sided: too few exceptions also fail. "Conservative" means the model currently overstates risk.
  • VaR says nothing about losses beyond it; ES fills part of that gap.
  • ECB rates are a daily 2:15 pm CET snapshot; intraday moves are not captured.

Quality checks on every load

Stop the load (nothing is written)

  • Valid dates and values
  • Rate > 0
  • No duplicate dates

Warnings (load continues, shown in the log)

  • Missing weekdays that are not TARGET holidays (ECB publishes on TARGET days only)
  • Weekend dates
  • Daily moves above 5%

Found on real data: until 2012 the ECB sends holidays as empty rows (status H). The adapter drops them; any other empty value still stops the load.

Operation

  • Initial: full history since 1999, rebuilt in one transaction.
  • Daily: last date minus 5 days, upsert on the date: running twice adds 0 rows.
  • Errors: 30 s timeout, 3 attempts with backoff, exit code 1 → alert.
  • Schedule: weekdays 16:30 CET after ECB publication, safety run 18:00 (cron / Task Scheduler; in the bank: Airflow or Control-M).

Design decisions

What was asked, what I built, and why.

1Many sources, clouds and legacy interfaces

What was asked

Data comes from many systems and clouds, and from older APIs. New sources must be easy to connect.

What I built

  • One adapter interface: every source returns the same two columns (date, rate).
  • ECB REST adapter (live) and one file adapter for local files, network shares, Amazon S3, Azure Blob/ADLS and Google Cloud Storage (fsspec).
  • The source is one line in config.py. Checks, upsert and load log are shared.
  • Task 2 joins two sources (CSV master data + Parquet prices) and resolves their conflicts: duplicate key, time zones, gaps.

Why

  • A new source is one small class; the ETL does not change.
  • Every load row names its source: full audit trail.
  • No credentials in code: each cloud uses its standard credential chain.
  • DuckDB can also read Parquet/CSV directly from S3 or Azure, so the same SQL works on a data lake.

2Clear and understandable at a glance

What was asked

The result must be clear immediately, without having to think, and every step from source to number must be traceable.

What I built

  • Status bar with five checks (data, load, tests, code, backtest): green or red.
  • Four KPI cards, a traffic light and one sentence in plain language.
  • Tabs by audience: board (Dashboard), risk (Risk Analytics, Index Analysis), data and IT (Data Pipeline, Quality), reviewers (Design Decisions).
  • Each number is stored with its inputs (fx_risk_history, etl_load_log).

Why

  • The board sees in five seconds whether there is a problem; detail is one click away.
  • Texts are generated from the numbers, so they can never contradict them.
  • Colour never stands alone: every status also has a word or icon.

3Modern, good tools

What was asked

Use modern technology - chosen on purpose, and fitting the problem.

What I built

ToolUsed for
Python 3.12+, pandas 3, pyarrowtransformations, Parquet
DuckDBembedded analytical SQL database, one file
fsspecone API for local files and all clouds
Plotlyinteractive charts, offline in one HTML file
pytest, ruffautomated tests and code checks
Git, GitHub Actionsversioning; tests and ruff on every push

Why

  • DuckDB: fast columnar SQL without a server; reads Parquet and cloud storage directly. Nothing to install or operate.
  • Static web page: no server, no login, works offline, can be mailed to the board.
  • Not chosen on purpose: Spark, Kubernetes, a database server. The data are small (7,000 rates, 143,000 index prices); more infrastructure would add cost, not value.
  • Ready to scale: the same SQL runs on a cloud warehouse; the daily run fits Airflow or Control-M; a container image is the next step.
